questions.stem: The word 'genocide' was coined in 1944 by the Polish-Jewish lawyer:
options: Raphael Lemkin
Hannah Arendt
Simon Wiesenthal
Primo Levi
questions.explanation: Lemkin combined the Greek 'genos' (race or tribe) with the Latin '-cide' (killing) in his book Axis Rule in Occupied Europe. He then campaigned for an international treaty. Arendt was a political theorist, Wiesenthal a Nazi-hunter and Levi an Auschwitz survivor and writer.

questions.stem: The UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide was adopted by the General Assembly in:
questions.explanation: The Convention was adopted on 9 December 1948, the day before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and came into force in 1951. It made genocide a crime under international law whether committed in war or peace.

questions.stem: Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, what must be proved for killings to count as genocide?
options: that more than one million people from a single country were killed in a war
that the killings were carried out by a government during an international war
that the victims were political opponents of the regime that killed them
intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
questions.explanation: The key element is specific intent to destroy a protected group as such. Political groups were left out of the final definition after objections from some states, including the Soviet Union, and there is no minimum number of victims.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes 'ethnic cleansing' from genocide?
options: Ethnic cleansing involves killing; genocide involves only forced removal of a group
Ethnic cleansing is a crime defined in the 1948 Convention; genocide is not
Ethnic cleansing happens only in peacetime; genocide happens only in war
Ethnic cleansing aims to remove a group from an area; genocide, to destroy it
questions.explanation: Ethnic cleansing means making an area ethnically uniform by forcing people out, often through violence and terror. It is not a separately defined crime but can be prosecuted as crimes against humanity, and it can overlap with or lead to genocide.

questions.stem: Gregory Stanton's model of the stages of genocide includes classification, symbolisation, dehumanisation and polarisation before extermination. Its main value for historians and policy makers is to:
options: measure how many people must die before an event can legally be called genocide
explain that genocides happen suddenly and cannot be predicted or prevented
show that genocide is a process with warning signs allowing intervention
prove that every genocide follows exactly the same order of events and timetable
questions.explanation: Stanton's model stresses that genocide develops over time, often beginning with labelling groups and hate propaganda. Critics note real cases do not follow a fixed sequence, but the model highlights opportunities for prevention.

questions.stem: Historians agree that the number of Jewish people murdered in the Holocaust was about:
options: three million
six million
one million
twelve million
questions.explanation: About six million Jews, roughly two-thirds of Europe's pre-war Jewish population, were murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. Millions of others were also killed, including Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war and Polish civilians.

questions.stem: From 1939-40 the Nazis forced Jews in occupied Poland into ghettos such as Warsaw and Łódź. The ghettos were:
options: camps outside Germany where Jews were trained for emigration to Palestine
factories where Jews worked for wages under protection from the German army
sealed districts where Jews were crowded together before deportation
neighbourhoods where Jews could live freely under their own elected governments
questions.explanation: Ghettos isolated Jewish communities behind walls or fences, and hunger and disease killed very many. From 1942 most inhabitants were deported to death camps. In April-May 1943 Jewish fighters in Warsaw staged the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.

questions.stem: Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka differed from concentration camps such as Dachau because they:
options: were run by the German army rather than by the SS and the police
were in Germany itself, while concentration camps were in occupied Poland
were built mainly to murder deported Jews on arrival
held political prisoners only, who were released when their sentences ended
questions.explanation: These were the camps of Operation Reinhard in occupied Poland, built to kill the Jews of the General Government. Auschwitz-Birkenau combined a forced-labour camp with a killing centre and was the largest site of murder.

questions.stem: International Holocaust Remembrance Day is held each year on 27 January because on that date in 1945:
options: Germany surrendered unconditionally to the Allies
the Nuremberg tribunal delivered its first verdicts
Jewish fighters began the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
Soviet troops reached the Auschwitz camp complex
questions.explanation: The UN General Assembly chose the date in 2005 to honour the victims. Germany surrendered on 7-8 May 1945, the Nuremberg verdicts came in October 1946, and the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began in April 1943.

questions.stem: The Nazi genocide of the Roma and Sinti is significant for a study of genocide because it shows that:
options: only Jewish victims are recognised in the 1948 Convention
the Roma were deported to Palestine rather than killed
Nazi racial policy also targeted other groups for destruction
the Nazis protected nomadic peoples as part of the German nation
questions.explanation: Roma and Sinti were persecuted as racially 'alien', deported and murdered in large numbers; Roma communities call the genocide the Porajmos. It was recognised slowly after the war, and survivors waited decades for acknowledgement.

questions.stem: In October 1943 most Danish Jews escaped the Nazis because:
options: Denmark's king paid Germany to release them to Switzerland
Danish people helped them flee by boat to neutral Sweden
the German army refused to carry out the deportation order
Britain sent warships to evacuate them across the North Sea
questions.explanation: Warned of a planned round-up, Danes hid their Jewish neighbours and fishermen ferried about 7,000 people to Sweden. It is the best-known example of a whole society acting as rescuers.

questions.stem: Christopher Browning's Ordinary Men (1992) and Daniel Goldhagen's Hitler's Willing Executioners (1996) both studied German police battalions. How did their explanations differ?
options: Browning blamed Hitler alone; Goldhagen argued that the killers were mainly non-German collaborators
Browning denied the killings took place; Goldhagen showed they were carried out only by the SS
Browning stressed situational pressures such as conformity; Goldhagen, deep German antisemitism
Browning argued the men were forced at gunpoint; Goldhagen argued they did not know what they were doing
questions.explanation: Browning found that men could refuse without severe punishment, yet most took part, which he explained through peer pressure, obedience and careerism. Goldhagen argued a distinctive 'eliminationist antisemitism' made Germans willing killers. The debate shapes how historians explain perpetrators.

questions.stem: After covering the 1961 trial in Jerusalem of Adolf Eichmann, who organised the deportation of Jews, Hannah Arendt described:
options: the 'banality of evil': ordinary bureaucrats could carry out great crimes
the 'final solution', the term Eichmann invented for the murder of Europe's Jews
the 'stab in the back', the myth that Jews had caused Germany's defeat in 1918
the 'master race', Hitler's belief in the superiority of the Aryan peoples
questions.explanation: Arendt saw Eichmann as a careerist who followed orders and procedures rather than a fanatic, a view later historians have challenged with evidence of his antisemitic commitment. The phrase remains central to debates about how genocide is carried out.

questions.stem: In 2000 a British court ruled against David Irving in a libel case he brought against historian Deborah Lipstadt. Why is the case significant for the study of the Holocaust?
options: The court found that Irving had distorted evidence to deny the Holocaust
The court ruled that historians may not write about the Holocaust without approval
The court decided the number of Holocaust victims was impossible to establish
The court found that the Nuremberg trials had been conducted unfairly
questions.explanation: Lipstadt had called Irving a Holocaust denier. Her defence, using expert historians, showed in detail how he had misrepresented sources, and the judge found that he was a denier who had manipulated evidence.

questions.stem: The Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia, led by Pol Pot, ruled from April 1975 until:
options: May 1975, after only a few weeks in power in the capital
1991, when the Paris Peace Accords were signed
1998, when Pol Pot died in the jungle near Thailand
January 1979, when Vietnam's army took Phnom Penh
questions.explanation: The regime, called Democratic Kampuchea, was overthrown when Vietnam invaded in December 1978 and took the capital on 7 January 1979. The Khmer Rouge kept fighting from the border regions for many years.

questions.stem: The Khmer Rouge's aim of a 'Year Zero' meant:
options: returning Cambodia to the rule of its king and the Buddhist monasteries of old
rapid industrialisation of Cambodia with aid from the United States
holding free elections every year to choose the country's leaders
remaking Cambodia as a classless rural society, wiping out the old order
questions.explanation: Money, markets, schools and religion were abolished and families separated in forced labour communes. People linked to the old order, including officials, teachers and city dwellers, were treated as enemies.

questions.stem: Deaths under the Khmer Rouge from execution, starvation, overwork and disease are usually estimated at:
options: about 6 million, more than the whole population of 1975
about 500,000, almost all of them ethnic Vietnamese residents
about 1.5 to 2 million, a fifth to a quarter of the people
about 100,000, mostly soldiers of the former Lon Nol government
questions.explanation: Estimates vary, but most fall in this range from a population of about 8 million. Victims included Khmers of all backgrounds as well as minorities such as the Cham Muslims and ethnic Vietnamese.

questions.stem: Tuol Sleng, a former Phnom Penh school also known as S-21, was:
options: the headquarters of the Vietnamese army after it captured Phnom Penh
the court where the Extraordinary Chambers tried Khmer Rouge leaders
a Khmer Rouge prison where thousands were held and very few survived
a refugee camp on the Thai border run by the United Nations after 1979
questions.explanation: Prisoners, many of them Khmer Rouge cadres accused of betrayal, were photographed and forced to confess before being killed. The regime's own records and photographs are now in the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum.

questions.stem: Through the 1980s the Khmer Rouge-led coalition kept Cambodia's seat at the United Nations. The best explanation is that:
options: the UN did not know about the killings until the Khmer Rouge leaders were tried in 2010
the Khmer Rouge won free elections held under UN supervision in 1981
the Soviet Union insisted on keeping Pol Pot's representatives in the General Assembly
Cold War politics led China, the US and ASEAN to oppose the Hanoi-backed regime
questions.explanation: Many states refused to recognise a government installed by Vietnam, a Soviet ally. Cold War alignment outweighed the evidence of mass killing, a stark example of the limits of international response.

questions.stem: Australia played a leading role in ending Cambodia's conflict through:
options: the resettlement of the entire Cambodian population in Australia
Gareth Evans's peace diplomacy and an Australian commanding UN forces
an Australian invasion in 1979 that drove the Khmer Rouge from Phnom Penh
trials of Khmer Rouge leaders held in Australian courts in the 1980s
questions.explanation: Evans's diplomacy contributed to the 1991 Paris Peace Accords, and Lieutenant General John Sanderson commanded the military component of the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), which oversaw the 1993 elections.

questions.stem: The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, a court set up with UN support, convicted senior Khmer Rouge leaders Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan of genocide in 2018. Taken together, the genocide findings concerned crimes against:
options: the Cham Muslims and ethnic Vietnamese
Cambodian soldiers of the Lon Nol government
American aircrew captured during the war
Thai traders living in the western provinces
questions.explanation: Most Khmer Rouge killing targeted people for political or class reasons, which the Convention does not cover, so these were prosecuted as crimes against humanity. The genocide charges focused on attempts to destroy ethnic and religious groups. Pol Pot died in 1998 without trial.

questions.stem: Which colonial practice helped harden the division between Hutu and Tutsi in Rwanda?
options: Belgian identity cards from the 1930s recording ethnic group
French laws banning marriage between Hutu and Tutsi from the 1950s
German policy of moving all Tutsi to neighbouring Uganda in 1914
British rule that gave Hutu chiefs control of Rwanda's government
questions.explanation: Belgian rulers favoured the Tutsi minority and issued cards stating ethnicity. In 1994 these cards were used at roadblocks to identify Tutsi. Rwanda was a German, then Belgian, colony and never British-ruled.

questions.stem: The genocide in Rwanda began in April 1994 immediately after:
options: the plane carrying President Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali
the Rwandan Patriotic Front captured the capital and seized power
UN peacekeepers withdrew completely from Rwanda at Belgium's request
Hutu and Tutsi leaders signed the Arusha peace agreement in Tanzania
questions.explanation: The president's death on 6 April was followed within hours by organised killings of Tutsi and moderate Hutu. The Arusha Accords had been signed in 1993; the RPF took Kigali in July 1994, ending the genocide.

questions.stem: Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM) contributed to the Rwandan genocide by:
options: calling on the Rwandan army to protect civilians from the militias
spreading hate propaganda calling Tutsi 'cockroaches' and naming targets
broadcasting UN warnings that encouraged Tutsi families to flee to safety
reporting on the genocide to international audiences in Europe and America
questions.explanation: RTLM dehumanised Tutsi and broadcast names and locations of targets. In 2003 the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda convicted media figures, showing that incitement through propaganda can itself be a crime.

questions.stem: Over about 100 days from April to July 1994, the Rwandan genocide killed:
options: several thousand soldiers of the Rwandan Patriotic Front
a few hundred political leaders in the capital, Kigali
millions of Hutu civilians in refugee camps in Zaire
hundreds of thousands of people, most of them Tutsi
questions.explanation: Estimates range widely, commonly from about 500,000 to 800,000 or more, killed largely by the Interahamwe militia, soldiers and ordinary civilians, often neighbours. The speed and the involvement of so many people set Rwanda apart.

questions.stem: Roméo Dallaire, commander of the UN mission in Rwanda (UNAMIR), is significant because he:
options: led the Rwandan Patriotic Front to victory over the government in July 1994
chaired the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in Arusha, Tanzania
warned the UN of planned killings in January 1994 but was told not to act
ordered his troops to leave Rwanda as soon as the genocide began in April 1994
questions.explanation: Dallaire's cable reporting arms caches and plans for extermination was not acted on, and his small force was later cut. His account, Shake Hands with the Devil, is a major source on the international failure.

questions.stem: During the Rwandan genocide, US officials avoided calling the events 'genocide' for weeks. Historians explain this mainly by:
options: a treaty with Rwanda that banned the United States from commenting on its affairs
the fact that the 1948 Convention had not yet been signed by the United States
the pressure to act that the word would create under the Convention
a lack of any reports of killings reaching Washington until July 1994
questions.explanation: Officials feared that naming genocide would create expectations of intervention, especially after the deaths of US soldiers in Somalia in 1993. The US had ratified the Convention in 1988. President Clinton later apologised for the failure to act.

questions.stem: In 1998 the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda convicted Jean-Paul Akayesu, a mayor. The judgement is significant because it was:
options: the first international genocide conviction, and it recognised rape as genocide
the first trial of a head of state for war crimes by an international court
the only case in which the tribunal found that no genocide had happened in Rwanda
a trial held in Rwanda by community courts without any judges or lawyers
questions.explanation: The tribunal sat in Arusha, Tanzania. Inside Rwanda, the huge number of suspects led to the community-based gacaca courts (2002-2012), which tried well over a million cases.

questions.stem: Australians served with the UN mission in Rwanda in 1994-95, mostly as:
options: pilots flying air strikes against militias
lawyers prosecuting cases at the tribunal
border guards stopping refugees leaving
medical staff and soldiers protecting them
questions.explanation: Australian medical teams and infantry served with the expanded UN mission after the genocide. In April 1995 they witnessed the Kibeho massacre at a camp for displaced people, an experience that has shaped Australian memory of peacekeeping.

questions.stem: During the Bosnian War (1992-95), 'ethnic cleansing' by Bosnian Serb forces mainly involved:
options: the voluntary exchange of populations agreed between the governments in 1992
the removal of Serbs from Bosnia by NATO forces after the Dayton Agreement
the resettlement of refugees from Kosovo in Bosnian towns after 1999
expelling Bosniaks and Croats through terror, detention camps and killing
questions.explanation: Bosnian Serb forces under Radovan Karadžić and General Ratko Mladić sought to create ethnically Serb territory. Croat forces also carried out ethnic cleansing in some areas, but the largest campaign was against Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims).

questions.stem: In July 1995, after Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN 'safe area' of Srebrenica:
options: UN troops drove the attackers out of the town
the Bosnian army took the city of Belgrade
the Dayton Agreement was signed in the town
about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed
questions.explanation: The lightly armed Dutch UN battalion did not resist the takeover. Courts have ruled that the killings at Srebrenica were genocide; it was the worst mass killing in Europe since the Second World War.

questions.stem: The siege of Sarajevo (1992-96) became a symbol of the Bosnian War because:
options: it was the only Bosnian city the Serbs captured during the war
UN troops fought a major battle there and defeated Serb forces
its population was evacuated safely at the start of the war
its civilians were shelled and sniped at for almost four years
questions.explanation: Bosnian Serb forces surrounded the capital, and thousands of civilians were killed while people queued for water or bread. It was the longest siege of a capital city in modern European history and was reported daily on world television.

questions.stem: The Bosnian War was ended by:
options: a referendum in which Bosnians voted to rejoin Yugoslavia
NATO air strikes in 1995 followed by the Dayton Agreement
a United Nations invasion that occupied Belgrade in 1994
the outright victory of Bosnian Serb forces in 1995
questions.explanation: After Srebrenica and a market shelling in Sarajevo, NATO's bombing campaign and a Croat-Bosniak offensive pushed the Serbs to negotiate. The agreement reached at Dayton, Ohio, in November 1995 divided Bosnia into two entities within one state.

questions.stem: In 2007 the International Court of Justice ruled in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro. What did it find?
options: Serbia was guilty of genocide across all of Bosnia and owed full compensation
Bosnia's government had committed genocide against Serbs in Sarajevo
Srebrenica was genocide; Serbia failed to prevent it but did not commit it
No genocide occurred in Bosnia, because the killings were part of a civil war
questions.explanation: The ICJ judges states, not individuals. It found Serbia had breached its duty to prevent genocide and to cooperate with the Yugoslavia tribunal, which separately convicted Karadžić (2016) and Mladić (2017) of genocide.

questions.stem: The 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P), endorsed at the UN World Summit in 2005, holds that:
options: if a state fails to protect its people from mass atrocities, others should act
every state has an absolute right to non-interference, whatever happens inside its borders
only the five permanent Security Council members may ever be tried for genocide
refugees fleeing genocide must be returned to their country once the fighting stops
questions.explanation: R2P was a response to the failures in Rwanda and Srebrenica. Any use of force still requires Security Council approval, so in practice it has often been blocked by vetoes.

questions.stem: The International Criminal Court, set up under the Rome Statute of 1998, differs from the tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda because it:
options: is permanent rather than created for a single conflict
can try states as well as individuals for genocide and war crimes
was created by the Security Council to try Nazi war criminals
can impose the death penalty on those convicted of genocide
questions.explanation: The ICC began work in 2002 in The Hague. In 2009-10 it issued arrest warrants for Sudan's president Omar al-Bashir, including for genocide in Darfur. The ICTY and ICTR were temporary tribunals, and none of these courts can impose the death penalty.

questions.stem: In 2017 more than 700,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar's Rakhine State for Bangladesh after a military campaign. The case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019 is significant because:
options: Myanmar's military leaders were arrested and tried in person by the ICJ in The Hague
it ended the conflict and allowed all Rohingya refugees to return home safely in 2019
Bangladesh was found guilty of genocide for refusing to admit Rohingya refugees
a state not directly affected used the Convention to hold another to account
questions.explanation: The Convention allows any party to bring a dispute about its obligations to the ICJ. The court ordered provisional measures to protect the Rohingya in 2020. Few refugees have been able to return.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the international response to genocide since 1948?
options: No one has ever been convicted of genocide by an international court since the Convention
Law and courts have grown, but prevention often failed when major powers would not act
The Genocide Convention has prevented any genocide from occurring since it came into force in 1951
The United Nations has intervened militarily within days in every case of genocide since 1948
questions.explanation: Tribunals, the ICC and R2P show real development in law and accountability, yet in Cambodia, Rwanda and Bosnia the world did not stop the killing. The other statements are false: genocides have occurred, and international courts have convicted many people.
